question: Which of these models is essentially unaffected by rescaling a feature?
options: k-nearest neighbors
A decision tree
An SVM with an RBF kernel
Ridge regression
explanation: A tree splits one feature at a threshold. Any monotonic rescaling just moves the threshold, so the splits and predictions are identical.

question: Why is mapping cities to 0, 1, 2, 3 a bad encoding for a linear model?
options: Linear models cannot read integers
It invents an order and spacing between cities that does not exist
It uses too many columns
It makes the model scale-invariant
explanation: A linear model treats the code as a quantity, implying city 3 is three times city 1. One-hot encoding gives each city its own independent weight.

question: A feature contains a few extreme outliers. Which scaler keeps the bulk of the values well spread out?
options: Min-max scaling
Standard scaling
Robust scaling with median and IQR
No scaling at all
explanation: The median and interquartile range ignore extreme values, so the normal points keep a sensible spread. Min-max and standard scaling are both stretched by the outliers.

question: When should you compute the mean and standard deviation used for standardization?
options: On the full dataset before splitting
On the test set, so test features are exactly mean 0
On the training data only, then apply them to validation and test data
Separately on each set, using each set's own statistics
explanation: Scaling statistics are learned parameters. Learning them from evaluation data leaks information; learning them separately per set makes the same raw value map to different numbers.

question: Why does standardizing features speed up gradient descent for linear regression?
options: It reduces the number of samples
It makes the loss surface closer to a round bowl, so one learning rate works well in every direction
It removes the need for an intercept
It turns the problem into classification
explanation: Features on very different scales create a long, narrow valley (a high condition number). The learning rate must be tiny for the steep direction, which makes progress along the flat direction extremely slow.

question: What does OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore") do with a category it did not see during fit?
options: Raises an error
Adds a new column at transform time
Encodes it as a row of all zeros
Maps it to the most frequent category
explanation: The unseen value matches none of the learned categories, so every indicator is 0. This keeps the output shape fixed for the downstream model.
